issues.legal_issue: The limitation period for a landlord’s application for possession begins when the tenancy is terminated, not when the tenant’s underlying breach occurs.
material_facts: The tenant defaulted on rent, with the last default occurring more than two years before the possession application.
The landlord served written notice terminating the tenancy on the ground of default, and the tenancy was properly terminated.
The landlord applied for possession within two years after the tenancy was terminated.
issues.conclusion: The application was within the limitation period because it was filed within two years of the tenancy’s termination; the appeal was allowed and the orders granting possession were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 14(1) and 29(2) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, the tenant’s breach alone does not terminate the tenancy or give the landlord the right to apply for possession. The right to apply accrues when the tenancy is terminated by the required notice, and the right to obtain possession is then deemed to have accrued for limitation purposes, although possession still requires an order. The Court relied on Raja Ram Mahadev Paranjype v. Aba Maruti Mali and approved Ramachandra Anant v. Janardan; it overruled Chimanbai Rama v. Ganpat Jagannath. The legislative history also supported termination as the starting point.

predicates.possession_application: A landlord applied to the competent authority for an order granting possession of land held by a tenant.
predicates.tenancy_terminated_by_notice: The landlord gave the required notice following a tenant’s breach, and the tenancy was terminated.
predicates.application_within_two_years_of_terminat: The landlord filed the possession application within two years after the tenancy was terminated.

issues.definition: When a landlord applies for possession after terminating a tenancy by notice and files within two years of termination, the application is not barred by limitation.
